C0.quote: computational aspects of the Chamberlin-Courant voting rule (CC)
C0.note: Winner determination algorithms for multiwinner voting rules.

C1.quote: runs in almost linear time in the input size

C2.1.quote: is called a preference profile or just a profile or preferences

C2.2.quote: a voter v gives an approval ballot as a vote
C2.2.note: Misrepresentation function r (cardinal) is the general input; linear orders, weak orders and approval ballots are special cases.

C2.3.quote: utility function u : V × C → R≥0 that indicates how well a voter
C2.3.note: Utilities/misrepresentation and preferences are mentioned, but they coincide with the input.

C2.4.quote: A tuple (V, C, r) or (V, C, u) is called a preference profile
C2.4.note: The input is described as preferences/misrepresentation and the rule is applied directly, with no statement about reporting.

C3.1.note: Pure winner-determination computation; no strategic voters.

C3.2.note: No statement that voters submit their held attitude.

C4.1.quote: u(v, c) = 1 iff c ∈ Av and u(v, c) = 0 iff c ∉ Av
C4.1.note: Approval utility is defined; for SP and Borda the misrepresentation r is the input itself. Thiele utility is defined from approvals.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.quote: total utility of the voters is maximized
C5.1.note: CC and Thiele rules are defined to minimise total misrepresentation or maximise total utility, and results are about computing the optimum.

C5.2.quote: we define total utility of C′ by u(C′) = Σ u(v, C′)
C5.2.note: Utility is evaluated directly on the input, with no statement relating it to held attitudes.

VOT.note: Voters are data of the input and take no action in the model.

C8.1.note: NA: no STRAT or MIXED type.

C9.1.note: The introduction mentions applications and practical efficiency of the algorithm, but makes no claims about voter well-being or which rule to use. The claim about the algorithm being efficient in practice concerns computation only.
